unit.title: Debt and credit
unit.description: What debt really costs, which kinds to avoid and how to get out of it

u3l1.title: Nominal rate, APR and the real cost of a loan

steps.title: Nominal rate and APR
steps.body:
• **Nominal rate (TIN in Spain):** the «pure» interest you're charged on the money you borrow.
• **APR (annual percentage rate; TAE in Spain):** adds the compulsory **fees** and takes into account how often you pay. It's the real cost over a year.

For consumer loans, the lender has to tell you the APR. To compare, always look at the APR.

steps.title: Why the APR is higher
steps.body:
If you pay every month, the interest compounds: a 12 % nominal rate with monthly payments works out as an **APR of 12.68 %**.

Fees push it up further. Over 3 years, a loan at a 6 % nominal rate with a 3 % arrangement fee costs more than one at a 7.5 % nominal rate with no fee: **an APR of 8.36 % versus 7.76 %**.

steps.title: Look at the payment and the interest
steps.body: Borrow €10,000 over 5 years at 7 %: you pay about €198 a month and about €1,881 in interest. Stretch it to 10 years: the payment drops to about €116… and the interest rises to about €3,933.
steps.tip: A low monthly payment isn't a cheap loan: it's usually a longer one.

steps.title: Not all debt is the same
steps.body:
• **Debt that can create value:** pays for something that lasts or earns you income, at a reasonable interest rate. An affordable mortgage, a cheap loan for training that boosts your salary.
• **Debt that destroys value:** funds spending that's over before the debt is, at a high interest rate. Holidays on instalments, the latest phone on a revolving credit card.

steps.title: Three questions before you sign
steps.body:
1. Will what I'm buying last longer than the debt?
2. What's the **APR**? Above 7-8 %, it's expensive debt.
3. Could I still pay if my income fell? The usual advice is that repayments on all your debts shouldn't go over **30-35 %** of your income.

steps.title: Even «good» debt has risks
steps.body: A mortgage is good debt only if the payment is affordable and you have a cushion. A master's degree on credit only creates value if it really does raise your income.
steps.key: Good debt: cheap and for something that lasts or earns income. Bad debt: expensive and for something that gets used up.
steps.tip: If you'll enjoy it for less time than it takes to pay off, think twice.

u3l3.title: Revolving credit cards and payday loans

steps.title: The revolving card
steps.body:
A revolving credit card lets you pay a **small fixed amount** each month. It seems convenient, but the payment barely covers the interest: the debt «renews» itself.

Their APRs are usually around **20 % or more**. In 2020 Spain's Supreme Court ruled that a revolving card with an APR of 26.82 % was usurious.

steps.title: The numbers
steps.body:
You owe €1,000 at a 24 % nominal rate (2 % a month) and pay €30 a month: in the first month €20 is interest and only €10 reduces the debt. It takes you **about 55 months** and you pay **about €1,664**. At €25 a month: about 81 months and over €2,000.

**Payday loans:** borrowing €300 and paying back €390 after 30 days works out as an APR of over **2,300 %**.

steps.title: How to get out
steps.body:
• Stop using the card.
• Raise the payment as much as you can.
• Once it's cleared, switch it to paying in full at the end of the month.
• If you think the interest is abusive, complain to the lender and, if they don't respond properly, to the Bank of Spain.
steps.key: The small payment is the bait: look at how much you owe and how much you pay in total.

steps.title: Two methods
steps.body:
With several debts, you pay the **minimum on all of them** and everything you have left over goes to just one:

• **Avalanche:** the one with the **highest interest** first. It costs you the least interest overall.
• **Snowball:** the one with the **smallest balance** first. You clear a debt quickly and that's motivating.

When you clear one, its payment gets added to the next: that's why it grows like a snowball.

steps.title: Which to choose?
steps.body:
On the numbers alone, the **avalanche** wins. But if you struggle to stick to the plan, the snowball gives you quick wins, and a plan you stick to beats a perfect one you give up on.

What doesn't work: spreading what's left over with no plan, or taking on another expensive debt to pay off the old ones.

steps.title: See how much interest weighs
steps.body: Enter €3,000 over 3 years at 22 %: about €1,125 in interest. Now at 6 %: about €286. That difference is what you save by tackling the expensive one first.

steps.title: The interest rate rule
steps.body:
Paying off a debt early gives you a **guaranteed return equal to its interest rate**.

• Debt at 20 %: paying it off is unbeatable. No investment guarantees 20 %.
• Debt above **7-8 %**: it almost always makes sense to pay it off before investing.
• Mortgage at 2-3 %: you can do both, pay it off and invest.

steps.title: What else counts
steps.body:
• **Guaranteed versus expected:** the stock market has returned more than 3 % in the long run, but with no guarantee and with years of falls.
• **Cushion first:** don't pay off debt with your emergency money.
• **Fees:** some mortgages charge for paying off early; check your contract.
• **Peace of mind:** owing less is worth something too.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Enter €5,000, €0 a month and 10 years at 3 %: that's what someone «earns» by paying off a 3 % mortgage, risk-free. Try 7 %: more, but with no guarantee at all.
steps.tip: These are examples, not promises: the stock market doesn't return the same every year.

u3l1-1.prompt: To compare loans you need to look at the ____, because it includes the fees.
u3l1-1.explanation: The APR covers the interest, the compulsory fees and how often you pay: it's the comparable cost.

u3l1-2.prompt: Loan A: 6 % nominal rate and a 3 % arrangement fee. Loan B: 7.5 % nominal rate with no fees. Same amount and term (3 years). Which is cheaper?
options: B, because its APR is lower
A, because its nominal rate is lower
u3l1-2.explanation: APR of A ≈ 8.36 %; of B ≈ 7.76 %. The arrangement fee makes A dearer even though its nominal rate is lower.

u3l1-3.prompt: You borrow €10,000 over 5 years at a 7 % nominal rate and pay €198.01 a month. How much do you pay in interest in total? (round it)
u3l1-3.explanation: 198.01 × 60 = €11,880.60; minus the €10,000 borrowed = about €1,881 in interest.

u3l1-4.prompt: The APR can never be higher than the nominal rate.
u3l1-4.explanation: It's usually higher: it adds fees and the effect of paying interest every month.

u3l1-5.prompt: Bruno is about to buy a car and the dealer offers him «a payment of only €149 a month». What does he do?
options: Asks for the APR, the term and the total he'll pay
Signs: he can afford €149 a month
Asks them to stretch the term even further so he pays less
u3l1-5.explanation: The payment on its own is misleading: what counts is the APR and the total to pay.
feedback: He finds out it's 84 payments: almost €12,520 in total. Now he can compare with other offers.
Being able to afford the payment says nothing about the cost: he could be paying for the car almost twice.
A lower payment, but more months paying interest.

u3l1-6.prompt: Quick: which figure includes the compulsory fees?
u3l1-6.explanation: The APR. The nominal rate is just the interest; Euribor is a benchmark index for variable-rate loans.

u3l1-7.prompt: Match each term with what it means.
u3l1-7.explanation: To compare loans: same amount, same term and the lowest APR.
right: The yearly cost with fees included
A payment on signing that pushes up the APR
Lower payment and more interest in total

u3l1-8.prompt: You borrow €20,000 at an 8 % nominal rate. Over 5 years you pay €4,332 in interest; over 8 years, €7,142. How much more do you pay by stretching it?
u3l1-8.explanation: 7,142 − 4,332 = €2,810 more for having a lower payment.

u3l1-9.prompt: A 12 % nominal rate with monthly payments works out as an APR of ____.

u3l1-10.prompt: What can make a loan more expensive? Tick all.
options: Paying it back early with no penalty
u3l1-10.explanation: Paying back early with no penalty cuts the interest: it's the only thing on the list that makes it cheaper.

u3l2-1.prompt: Does this debt usually create or destroy value?
options: Holidays paid with a revolving card
A cheap loan for a vocational course (FP) that raises your salary
A €1,200 phone over 24 months with interest
A birthday dinner deferred on a card at 20 %
u3l2-1.explanation: The key question: does what you buy last, or earn, more than the debt costs?

u3l2-2.prompt: Match each debt with its description.
u3l2-2.explanation: The interest rate and what the money is used for decide whether a debt helps or sinks you.
right: Expensive debt that drags on endlessly
Quick money at a sky-high cost
A home that lasts longer than the debt

u3l2-3.explanation: Only if the payment is affordable and you have a cushion. A mortgage you can't pay is a huge problem.

u3l2-4.prompt: A debt at 20 % APR is expensive debt.
u3l2-4.explanation: Well above 7-8 %: you need to get rid of it as soon as possible.

u3l2-5.prompt: Marta, 24, wants to go to Japan. The trip costs €3,000 and she's offered finance over 2 years at 14 % APR. What does she do?
options: Pays with her revolving credit card
Takes the finance: that way she travels now
Saves €250 a month and travels in a year's time
u3l2-5.explanation: For wants, it's better to save first than to owe afterwards.
feedback: With an APR of around 20 % or more, the trip could cost her much more, and for years.
She'll be paying for the trip for two years, with about €430 in interest: the memory lasts less than the debt.
She travels a year later, with no interest and no payments waiting when she gets back.

u3l2-6.prompt: You take home €1,800. If your debt repayments shouldn't go over 35 % of your income, what's the most you can pay a month?

options: A revolving card to pay for a trip
A mortgage with a payment of 25 % of your income
A payday loan for a concert
u3l2-7.explanation: Cheap, for something that lasts and with an affordable payment.

options: Great, that way you won't notice it!
Look at the APR and how much you'll pay in total
Better get a €2,000 one, the payment barely goes up
u3l2-8.explanation: Before financing a treat, multiply the payment by the number of months.
feedback: You will notice: 60 × 24 = €1,440. You pay €240 more for something that will be worth much less in 2 years.
Nice! 60 × 24 = €1,440: €240 in interest. Saving up for a few months might work out better.
That only stretches the debt for something that loses value very quickly.
lines: I want to buy the new €1,200 phone 📱
The shop will finance it over 24 months, only €60 a month!

u3l2-9.prompt: Pablo can borrow €6,000 at 6 % APR for a certified course after which, in his sector, salaries usually rise by about €300 a month. He has a cushion. What does he do?
options: Puts it on the revolving card so as not to take out a loan
Borrows €10,000 to treat himself to something too
Checks the payment fits his budget and takes the loan
u3l2-9.explanation: The same debt can be good or bad: it depends on the cost and what it gives you back.
feedback: Same purchase, but at a much higher interest rate.
He mixes a debt that creates value with one that destroys it.
If the pay rise comes, the debt pays for itself in a short time: it's debt that can create value.

u3l3-1.prompt: You owe €1,000 on a revolving card at 2 % a month. How many euros of interest do you pay in the first month?

u3l3-2.prompt: Quick: you pay a €30 instalment and €20 of it is interest. How much does your debt go down that month?
u3l3-2.explanation: 30 − 20 = €10. Only a third of what you pay reduces the debt.

u3l3-3.prompt: Tick the messages that are a debt trap or a scam.
options: You've switched your card to paying in full at the end of the month. No more interest will be charged for deferring.
Congratulations! Pay for all your purchases in easy instalments of just €25 a month. Activate it now.
We'll cancel all your debts. You just have to pay €200 in admin fees upfront by Bizum.
€300 in 10 minutes, no paperwork, no questions asked! Pay back just €390 in 30 days.
Reminder: your loan has 14 payments left. APR: 7.2 %.
u3l3-3.explanation: Instant money with no questions, minimum payments that hide the debt and upfront payments to «cancel debts» are warning signs.

u3l3-4.prompt: Why is a revolving card so expensive?
options: Because it charges a fee on every purchase in shops
Because it can only be used outside Spain
Because the small payment barely reduces the debt and the interest piles up
u3l3-4.explanation: With a €30 payment on €1,000 at 2 % a month, only €10 reduces the debt in the first month.

u3l3-5.prompt: Switching your card to paying in full at the end of the month avoids paying interest for deferring.
u3l3-5.explanation: You pay what you've spent in one go, with no deferral and no interest.

u3l3-6.prompt: Ana owes €2,000 on a revolving card at 22 % APR and pays €50 a month. She has €4,000 in an account at 2 %, and her ideal cushion is €2,000. What does she do?
options: Invests the €4,000 in the stock market to earn more than 22 %
Uses €2,000 to clear the revolving card and keeps €2,000 as a cushion
u3l3-6.explanation: Paying off expensive debt is the best guaranteed «investment» there is.
feedback: No investment guarantees 22 %; the debt, on the other hand, definitely charges it.
She saves a guaranteed 22 % and still has a cushion: she wins on every front.
She earns 2 % in the account while paying 22 % on the card: she loses about €400 a year.

u3l3-7.prompt: What helps you get out of a revolving card? Tick all.
options: Paying it off with a payday loan
Asking to switch it to paying at the end of the month
u3l3-7.explanation: Paying off an expensive debt with an even more expensive one only makes the problem worse.

u3l3-8.prompt: Quick: which debt is the most expensive?
u3l3-8.explanation: The revolving card: almost three times the personal loan and over seven times the mortgage.

u3l3-9.prompt: A €300 payday loan where you pay back €390 after 30 days has an APR of over ____.
u3l3-9.explanation: 30 % in one month, compounded over a year, is over 2,300 %.

options: Yes, that way you don't stress
Get another card to pay this one off
Careful: with that payment it's almost all interest
u3l3-10.explanation: A comfortable payment can hide a debt that lasts for years.
feedback: With €1,000 at 2 % a month, at €25 a month you'd take about 81 months and pay over €2,000.
Then you'd have two expensive debts instead of one.
That's it! Raise the payment as much as you can and stop using it until it's paid off.
lines: My card lets me pay just €25 a month of what I owe 😌

u3l4-1.prompt: Avalanche method: put in order which debt you tackle first.
u3l4-1.explanation: In the avalanche, the interest rate rules: highest to lowest.

u3l4-2.prompt: Snowball method with the same debts: put them in order from first to last.
u3l4-2.explanation: In the snowball, the balance rules: smallest to largest.

u3l4-3.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
u3l4-3.explanation: In both methods you pay the minimum on all of them and put the extra into one.
right: What you pay on all the others
The freed-up payment is added to the next one

u3l4-4.prompt: You owe €1,200 on a revolving card at 22 % a year. How much interest do you save in a year if you clear it now? (approximate, simple interest)

u3l4-5.prompt: Quick: you clear the instalment purchase, which had a €90 payment. You were paying €150 on the revolving card. How much do you pay on it each month now?
u3l4-5.explanation: 150 + 90 = €240: the freed-up payment is added to the next debt.

u3l4-6.prompt: Pablo has tried the avalanche twice and given up: his big debt never seems to end and he loses heart. What does he do?
options: Takes out a payday loan to pay it all off in one go
Stops paying the big one for a while
Tries the snowball to get some motivation
u3l4-6.explanation: The best method is the one you manage to stick to.
feedback: He swaps several debts for one extremely expensive one: the problem grows.
Surcharges, late-payment interest and possibly ending up on a bad-debtor register.
He clears two small debts in a few months and gets his drive back. He pays a little more interest, but he doesn't give up.

u3l4-7.prompt: Laura gets a €1,000 bonus. She owes €1,000 on a revolving card at 21 % and €4,000 on her car at 6 %. What does she do with the bonus?
options: Splits it half and half between the two
u3l4-7.explanation: With extra money, the first debt to go is the one with the highest interest.
feedback: She gets rid of the most expensive debt and frees up that payment for the car.
She keeps the 21 % debt alive: she pays expensive interest she could have avoided.
She saves 6 % when she could have saved 21 %.

u3l4-8.prompt: The snowball is always the method that makes you pay the least interest.
u3l4-8.explanation: That's the avalanche. The snowball sacrifices a bit of money in exchange for motivation.

u3l4-9.prompt: Quick: in the avalanche, what do you look at to choose?
u3l4-9.explanation: The interest: the most expensive debt first.

u3l4-10.prompt: What's a bad idea if you have several debts? Tick all.
options: Stopping paying the minimum on one of them
Paying the minimum on all and the extra on one
Carrying on buying with the revolving card
Taking out a payday loan to pay off the card
u3l4-10.explanation: Paying the minimum on all and putting the extra into one is exactly the basis of both methods.

u3l5-1.explanation: Above 7-8 %, paying off usually wins; with cheap debt there's room to decide.

u3l5-2.prompt: You pay €3,000 off a loan at 9 % early. Roughly how much interest do you save in the first year?

u3l5-3.prompt: Bruno has a fixed-rate mortgage at 2 %, a 6-month cushion and another €10,000 saved that he won't need for 15 years. What does he do?
options: Takes out another loan to invest more
Compares the guaranteed 2 % from paying off with long-term, diversified investing, without touching his cushion
Puts it all into a single trendy share because the mortgage is cheap
u3l5-3.explanation: With cheap debt there's no single right answer: what matters is comparing properly and not touching the cushion.
feedback: Borrowing to invest multiplies the risk.
He understands what he gains with each option and can split between the two.
A single company can collapse: that's not comparing, it's gambling.

u3l5-4.prompt: Marta has €3,000 on a revolving card at 21 % and another €3,000 she wants to start investing in a fund. What does she do first?
options: Invests the €3,000 and keeps paying the card
Invests half and pays off half
u3l5-4.explanation: Investing with a 21 % debt is filling a leaky bucket.
feedback: She locks in a risk-free 21 % a year. Then she invests what she used to pay each month.
To come out ahead, the fund would have to return more than 21 % a year.
Better than nothing, but it keeps a 21 % debt alive.

u3l5-5.prompt: Paying off a debt at 20 % is the same as a guaranteed 20 % return.
u3l5-5.explanation: Every euro you pay back stops costing you 20 % a year.

u3l5-6.prompt: It's a good idea to use your emergency fund to pay off your mortgage.
u3l5-6.explanation: The cushion is for the unexpected; if you spend it, the next scare ends up as expensive debt.

u3l5-7.prompt: You have a debt at 4 %. What does paying it off give you?
options: Nothing, because you don't earn interest
u3l5-7.explanation: What you no longer pay is a guaranteed gain equal to the interest rate.

u3l5-8.prompt: Your fixed-rate mortgage charges a 0.5 % fee for paying off early. You pay off €10,000. How much is the fee?
u3l5-8.explanation: 10,000 × 0.005 = €50. Always check your contract before paying off early.

options: Invest in whatever has gone up most this year
Always pay it off: debt is bad
It depends: compare the guaranteed 2 % with investing for the long term, and check you have a cushion
u3l5-9.explanation: Paying off gives a guaranteed return; investing, an expected one. With cheap debt, both options can make sense.
feedback: That's not comparing: it's chasing trends.
Not always: at 2 % it's cheap debt. It depends on your cushion, your time horizon and your peace of mind.
That's it: with cheap debt there's no single answer; what matters is understanding what you're comparing.
lines: I've got a mortgage at 2 % and €200 a month left over.
Should I pay it off or invest?

u3l5-10.prompt: Put the usual priorities for your money in order.
u3l5-10.explanation: The money pyramid: without a base, any surprise forces you to sell at the worst moment.
